title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
hook: a shepherd boy with a sling and no armor faces a giant

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's harp, and a king whose dark lifted. Your line was music lifts. Today, the same shepherd, with a very different tool in his hand.

Two armies on two mountains, a valley between them. Morning and evening, a Philistine champion named Goliath walks out into that valley in a bronze helmet and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam, and shouts: choose a man, and let him come down to me. Saul and all Israel are dismayed and greatly afraid. Into this walks the youngest son of Jesse, sent by his father to bring bread to his older brothers at the front. He hears the challenge, and asks: who is this, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE VALLEY.` → `CHOOSE A MAN, AND LET HIM COME.` → `A BOY BRINGING BREAD.`

segments.voice: His oldest brother, Eliab, is furious: why did you come down here? I know your pride. But word reaches Saul, and David says: your servant will go and fight him. You're a boy, says Saul, and he's been a man of war since his youth. David answers from experience. When a lion or a bear took a lamb from the flock, I went after it and took the lamb from its mouth. The LORD who saved me from the lion and the bear will save me from this Philistine. So Saul dresses David in his own armor: a bronze helmet, a coat of mail, a sword. David tries to walk, and can't. I haven't tried these, he says, and takes them off. This is the heart of the story. He doesn't go out in the king's equipment, pretending to be a soldier. He goes out as what he is. He takes his staff, and "chose him five smooth stones out of the brook," puts them in his shepherd's bag, sling in hand. Goliath mocks him. David answers: you come to me with a sword and a spear, "but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts," for the battle is the LORD's. He runs toward the Philistine, takes one stone, slings it, and it sinks into Goliath's forehead, and he falls on his face. The text even notes there was no sword in David's hand. He picked five, and needed one.
screen: `THE LION, THE BEAR, THE LAMB.` · `SAUL'S ARMOR DOESN'T FIT.` · `IN THE NAME OF THE LORD OF HOSTS.` · `HE PICKED FIVE, AND NEEDED ONE.` · then, large: `FIVE SMOOTH STONES OUT OF THE BROOK.`

segments.voice: Name one giant in your valley right now, a debt, a hard conversation, a project you can't start, and notice whether you've been fighting it in someone else's armor. Then ask what your smooth stones are, the small things you already know how to do, and choose one. If you pray, bring the giant to God as David did.
smooth stones. What David chose from the brook when he set aside Saul's armor to face Goliath with a sling. He picked five; one was enough.
Your line: one was enough. He went out as what he was. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Jews read David and Goliath as part of the Former Prophets, and many readers take it as a story of courage and of trust in God.

chat.says: How did David beat a giant? Did he wear really strong armor?
options: He took off Saul's armor and went as a shepherd: a sling, five stones, God's name.
Yes, Saul's armor fit him well and kept Goliath's spear from hurting him.
He threw all five stones, one after another, until Goliath finally fell.
chat.meaning: Saul's armor didn't fit, so David went with his staff, sling and five stones, in the name of the LORD. One stone was enough.

notes: Audit: 17:40 and 17:45 were cited to the KJV on the Judaism path; the fragments are believed identical in JPS 1917 and are now cited there (verify). howItsDone's unsourced 'taught to children and adults alike' softened.
Quotations from 17:40 and 17:45 use the KJV, which matches the JPS 1917 in these fragments as far as the writer recalls; confirm and switch the citation to JPS 1917 if identical.
'Five' is in 17:40; 'one stone' is in 17:49; 'no sword in the hand of David' is in 17:50. Goliath's height, the weight of his armor and the forty days (17:4–7, 17:16) are deliberately left out.
Saul's 'a man of war from his youth' (17:33), the lion and the bear (17:34–37), Eliab's rebuke (17:28) and David's 'I haven't tried them' (17:39) are paraphrased without quotation marks.
The practice's list ('a debt, a diagnosis...') is illustrative; a Keeper may want to soften 'diagnosis'.
